source.title: Beware of the Batch Size: Hyperparameter Bias in Evaluating LoRA

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies batch size and reports held-out task accuracy under fixed-sample and fixed-step protocols. Its results refine the large-batch claim: the trend depends on data scale and training protocol, and an optimal batch size exists.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out accuracy, not training error or the training–test gap. The batch-size accuracy results bear on V5. The optimal-learning-rate trajectory in Figure 5 is not a separate row because it is a hyperparameter-selection result; cited findings from other studies are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study tests V5 in a new setting: language-model LoRA fine-tuning with batch-size sweeps, independently tuned learning rates, one training epoch, and held-out accuracy. Appendix B explicitly reports degradation under this fixed-sample protocol. Non-monotonic performance and dataset-dependent thresholds are consistent with V5, which already specifies a workload-dependent batch-size threshold.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but omits a central conclusion: properly tuned vanilla LoRA matches or outperforms the tested variants, whose reported advantages can reflect batch-size choices. The authors also conclude that batch performance is non-monotonic and that lower-rank, smaller-model proxies can guide tuning when the target dataset size is preserved.
record.recipe_differences: LoRA fine-tuning of language models with batch-size sweeps and GSM8K or HumanEval evaluation, rather than the claim's natural-label memorization/generalization experiments or image-classifier settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch-size outcomes vary with dataset scale and training protocol; the authors report broadly consistent trends across rank and model capacity. Learning-rate scheduling changes accuracy, and the warm-up phase has marginal performance effects.

fits_no_version.finding: With 200 optimization steps, increasing batch size improves held-out accuracy before gains diminish, while also increasing processed data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under a fixed update budget, larger batches can improve LoRA fine-tuning accuracy through increased data exposure, with diminishing returns.

record.problems: Most batch-specific accuracy values are presented only in figures; no error bars or statistical tests are stated. The fixed-step result changes the amount of data processed as batch size changes, and the tested setting is LoRA supervised fine-tuning rather than the original image-classification setting.
record.rows_left_out: No results meeting the row criteria were left out. The optimal-learning-rate trajectory in Figure 5 was a hyperparameter-selection result and is not a held-out accuracy outcome.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out generalization in the same architectures and recipes.
Network-width sweeps beyond zero training error; adapter-rank sweeps do not measure this.
Convolutional versus fully connected image architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons; AdamW is used without such a comparison.

Image classification and full-parameter training; controlled recovery through longer training at a fixed batch size; normalization or regularization changes; whether learning-rate scaling with warm-up removes the penalty. Learning rates are independently tuned, but no scaling-rule recovery comparison is reported.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on dataset size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap correlations, and comparisons with other measures.
Removing memorized examples versus random removals and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: No challenges verdict is warranted from the fixed-step experiment because its training budget differs from V5's fixed-epoch condition. An optimal batch size and dataset-dependent tolerance do not limit a claim that already includes workload-dependent thresholds. Exact thresholds and batch-specific accuracies cannot be reconstructed from the supplied figure text. The study is not an original source for V5.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image models.

Image classifiers; comparisons with small-batch training in full-parameter models; normalization or regularization changes; learning-rate scaling with warmup; results under equal epoch budgets for other model types.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2-7B
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned on MetaMathQA; one epoch under fixed sample protocol
rows.operation_detail: Swept batch size and learning rate for vanilla LoRA, PiSSA, and MiLoRA; evaluated GSM8K accuracy.
rows.value: Batch-size selection alone can induce a performance gap of over 10% in final accuracy; vanilla LoRA achieves the best overall result when hyperparameters are optimally tuned.
rows.uncertainty: Figures are averaged over three random seeds, except Figures 3, 4, and 5; no error bars or statistical tests stated.
rows.note: The text reports the qualitative result; the batch-specific accuracy values are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: The recorded accuracy spread alone does not establish its direction. Add the fixed-sample degradation described in Appendix B and the optimal-batch finding in Section 3.2. Separate the LoRA-versus-variant ranking from the batch-size outcome; that ranking does not test V5.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2-7B
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned on MetaMathQA; one epoch under fixed sample protocol
rows.operation_detail: Compared batch-size accuracy trends across LoRA ranks 32, 64, 128, and 256.
rows.measure: Shifted GSM8K accuracy across batch sizes
rows.baseline: Default configuration: rank 128, dataset scale 100K, model capacity 7B; maxima shifted to match it.
rows.value: The fundamental performance trend remains consistent across evaluated ranks, with minor variations.
rows.uncertainty: Three-seed average; no error bars or statistical tests stated.
rows.note: Exact accuracy values are in figures; the text says increasing rank beyond a threshold yields marginal gains.
rows.check: The consistent batch-size trend across ranks is an instance of the fixed-sample degradation, not evidence that V5 appears only partially. Shifted accuracies preserve within-configuration batch-size differences but cannot establish absolute accuracy differences between ranks.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2-7B
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned on MetaMathQA for 200 optimization steps
rows.operation_detail: Swept batch size with optimization steps fixed at 200.
rows.value: Larger batches lead to superior performance as increased data outweighs the potential impact of batch size; gains reach a point of diminishing returns.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 3 is not stated to be averaged across seeds; no error bars or statistical tests stated.
rows.note: The text says batch size 512 corresponds to approximately one epoch. Exact plotted values appear only in the figure.
rows.check: Holding updates fixed changes the number of processed samples with batch size. This does not test the fixed-epoch penalty or demonstrate recovery by extending training at the same batch size. It cannot justify a challenges verdict on V5.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2-7B
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned on MetaMathQA; one epoch under fixed sample protocol
rows.operation_detail: Compared batch-size accuracy curves with and without warm-up and learning-rate scheduling.
rows.baseline: Default configuration; exact value not stated.
rows.value: Removing warm-up maintains robust performance without significant accuracy loss; learning-rate scheduling significantly influences accuracy, with its removal resulting in approximately 5% accuracy degradation.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 4 is not stated to be averaged across seeds; no error bars or statistical tests stated.
rows.note: This is a recipe condition affecting batch-size performance; exact plotted values appear only in the figure.
rows.check: Warm-up and scheduling are relevant recipe changes, but the approximately 5% scheduling effect is an overall accuracy difference, not a measured reduction of the large-batch penalty. The text does not quantify whether either change closes the small-versus-large-batch difference. Distinguish the scheduler and warm-up ablations.

relationships.condition: One-epoch fixed-sample LoRA fine-tuning on MetaMathQA, with learning rate tuned separately for each batch size; LLaMA-2 rank, dataset-size, and model-capacity sweeps.
relationships.reason: R1–R4 report an optimal batch range and consistent batch-size trends, with larger datasets tolerating larger batches; Appendix B explicitly identifies degradation in the fixed-sample experiments. This matches V5's workload-dependent threshold.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy degraded beyond an optimal batch range despite separate learning-rate tuning. Across the tested ranks and model capacities, larger datasets tolerated larger batches.

source_check.notes: Appendix B attributes part of the fixed-sample penalty to fewer updates; fixed-step gains involve more processed data. The shared-author flag warrants checking: paper author Jaeho Lee and cited original author Jaehoon Lee have different names.

statements.correction: One-epoch MetaMathQA experiments; consistent batch-size trends across LLaMA-2-7B and 13B; fixed-sample degradation explicitly reported in Appendix B. Supplied header marks one shared author. Paper authors: Sangyoon Lee and Jaeho Lee.
